utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, you are to continue with your opening.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have no lectern today?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, I was told that I was not coming very clearly and I think my movements and shifting away from the mikes was part of the problem so I figured I would take the centre chair for the microphone. I must admit it's a little difficult when you're feeling something and time of course constraints and the next court session causes what we have to take this break, but I hope I can pick up where I left off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I think it's really important at this time, Your Honour, to focus, Your Honours, to focus on the first two incidents. I think the Prosecution is placing them forward because they feel that maybe it's the simplest and the strongest cases against Mr. Lukic. I respectfully disagree. As I stated yesterday, I think that a simple but graphic inconsistency between two of the eye witnesses should be enough, under the principles of reasonable doubt, to bring into question the entire allegations as to the Drina River. It seems insurmountable with three witnesses, include a co-accused, Mitar Vasiljevic, pointing the finger at Milan Lukic, but clearly, from the transcripts of the earlier trial, from the tactics of the Vasiljevic Defence, Mr. Lukic was simply an empty chair which it was easy to point fingers at because there was no one to defend Mr. Lukic's position at that point in time and that's common amongst criminal Defence lawyers when you have a separation of trials is to attempt to point the blame at other co-accused or unindicted co-conspirators in an attempt to mitigate or eliminate culpability. When we look at the Drina River incident, I am confident, following the cross-examination and examination of the evidence you will find Mr. Milan Lukic not guilty of the Drina River incident. When you move on to the Pionirska Street fire, that is an extremely tragic and serious incident of which I think the Prosecution is right to bring into light the tragedy; but to implicate someone for this horrible event is also, as serious I think an accusation as can come before any Tribunal, anywhere, mass murder, with reckless indifference for the rights of those inside, and so to point those fingers, I think you still must also examine the intentions of those that might do so. As I stated, Mr. Lukic, his cousin and Mitar were all local citizens which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: My I interrupt you for a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I neglected to say in the beginning that in the absence of Judge Christine Van Den Wyngaert, Judge David and I sit pursuant to the provisions of Rule 15 bis. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. When you look at the fire and you hear the screams of the victims, I know the Prosecution, and I think even yourselves, might want to find someone responsible. There needs to be, the victims demand it, the process has gone on for so long, so -- and the problem is people have been saying Milan Lukic is guilty of there for so long, it's hard not to believe it. And so I will point to the alibis presented by Mitar Vasiljevic as an incredible problem with the case. Because as I stated, Milan Lukic and Mitar Vasiljevic were identified together. They were identified by people that claimed they knew them and knew them for a time being part of this community, and yet when one is is absolutely proven, I think, not to be there, it brings into suspect the entire situation. You add to that the Milan Lukic at 23 years old simply would not have had the rank or experience to make these sorts of decisions in total. Even though the regular army had retreated from the town at this point, they were still in the area and to think that local policemen, local Serb paramilitaries are not -- were responsible for this, for ordering this, for planning this, I think ignores the normal chains of command in this sort of situation. At best, Milan Lukic was a pawn to those above him of those of more social status, experience, age and importance. He was there because his family was there and they, as much as anyone here, needed to be out of this war zone. Milan Lukic was never charged in any court for these crimes, and as I stated the UN report never mentions these incidents despite the fact that there were from due diligence by the United Nations taken in 93 to 95. The statements that brought about these questions occurred much later, and I think just in terms of recollection of time, place and a real desire of the victims and witnesses to point the finger makes the easiest route to Milan Lukic. As such, Your Honour, I will close my closing statement and basically reserve for the remainder of the counts as we are still in the process of preparation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Alarid. Mr. Groome, your first witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the first witness is outside, if I could raise a couple of matters with the Chamber before he enters the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: First, Your Honour I would like to work with the witness with two aerial photographs they were photographs that were shown yesterday during the opening statement. They were taken several months ago and were disclosed to the Defence counsel shortly after they were taken, a matter of days, if not a week. The Prosecutor -- Prosecution is in the process of putting all of these photographs into a single exhibit, a computer programme which will allow the Chamber to look at any of the sites that are discussed in -- over the course of the trial and will give the Trial Chamber the capacity to look around and view the sites. That exhibit is not yet prepared, but I would like to use two of those photographs today. I've spoken with Mr. Alarid and Mr. Cepic and they have no objection to me using them, but I would like to seek the Court's permission because they are not yet formally on the exhibit list at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, very well, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour and the Prosecution calls VG-014.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we filed this morning a motion for leave to extends the normal allotment for cross-examination if need be and based on earlier 92 bis and 92 ter objections, we feel that cross-examination should be greater than the normal 60 per cent of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will certainly allow that if need be. If you need more than the 60 per cent, you'll get it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: As long as you're not wasting time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I would expect the Court to correct me if I'm being cumulative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Very well, Mr. Groome, you had called a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Prosecution calls VG-014, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we please go into private session to bring in the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I should say with the indulgence of the interpreters I'd like the first session to conclude at 4 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are a couple of bookkeeping matters I'd like to raise with the Chamber, perhaps we could make productive use of the time while the witness is being brought in. Your Honour, the first is a clarification with respect to 92 ter witnesses that the Prosecution anticipates we will need more than the 30 minutes directed by the Court. Does the Court expect a written application or is it sufficient that we make oral applications prior to the witness being called?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Make it orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour. And then the other matter which -- there have been varying practices with respect to exhibits attached to testimony of 92 ter submissions. Some Chambers have accepted all of the exhibits that have the witnesses have referred to in their transcript, I note from the Chamber's recent decision that it made some distinction between exhibits in that some were on the exhibit list and some were not, and I guess what I'm seeking clarification about is whether the Chamber would like the Prosecution to make formal application separate and apart from the 92 ter application for those exhibits that are referred to in the course of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If they are not on the 65 ter list then you should make a separate application.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just to give the Court an example of the type of exhibit I'm speaking about, many of the witnesses in the Vasiljevic case during the course of their testimony drew diagrams. The Prosecution did not make a formal application to add those diagrams but made the perhaps incorrect assumption that if the Court accepted their testimony in written form they would also accept the diagrams because the testimony is essentially indecipherable without the accompanying diagram.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I believe a separate application should be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Then the Prosecution will do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I believe we are still in private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session? Yes. Public session, let's go into public session, then.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I note that the blinds are still down. Your Honour, this witness is the subject of protective measures, and I'd ask the usher to please hand a pseudonym sheet to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Witness VG-014, the usher is now showing you a sheet. I'd ask you to take a look at it and ask you is that your name on that sheet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is that your date of birth on that sheet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask you to sign your name to that sheet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The Chamber has ordered certain protective measures with respect to you and these are that we shall refer to you as VG-014 during the course of your testimony and the image of your face will be distorted so that you cannot be recognised. If you look down on that sheet, there is a name of a person with the pseudonym of VG-032 next to the name. Is that the name of a person who you are likely to refer to in the course of your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour at this time I would tender the pseudonym sheet into evidence as a sealed exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours the exhibit will become P1 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: VG-014, in the spring of 1992, can you describe for us where in general terms you lived, not your house address, but the area in which you lived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: In 1992, I lived at Bikavac, which is a neighbourhood distant from the centre of the town of Visegrad, some 300 to 500 metres. I lived there with my family, with my wife and my minor daughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How old was your daughter at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: At that time, my daughter was three and a half years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time in the spring of 1992 that you left with your family, you left your home in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What is your best memory of when you left your home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: I believe that that was in March or April 1992, when I left and went to Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you familiar with an event in which a large amount of water was released from the hydroelectric dam south of the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When did you leave in relation to that event?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: I left immediately after that event. I left town immediately thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And why did you decide to leave Visegrad and go to Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Well, you know, the Uzice Corps was about to enter Visegrad, and we were afraid of it. We were scared that it might commit some wrongdoings and for the sake of my own safety, I left the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you returned to Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And around when, approximately when was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: I think that it was at the end of April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what made you decide to return to Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Well, I decided to do that because the then-authorities probably in negotiations with the then-authorities of Visegrad, decided to send us back because ostensibly, our security was guaranteed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was there any announcement made with respect to people's jobs and the necessity for them to return?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Well, you see, there was no written notice to that effect, but it was said orally that whosoever failed to return to their jobs would be fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you said orally, how did you learn about this statement that people would be fired if they did not return to their jobs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Well, quite a few of us had the work obligation, so one could hear such stories, a colleague would tell a colleague and that colleague another colleague and so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How did you get back to Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: This was organised, the return to Visegrad was organised, by buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you return with your wife and your child?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a point in time in your return to Visegrad where the bus was stopped?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes. At a number of check-points, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to focus on the first one? Can you tell us where it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: The first check-point was at the settlement of Medzedza. There we were stopped and we were ordered out of the bus and we were told to take out of the bus all our things, to open our bags, and to pour the content of the bags on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And where was this first check-point in relation to the town centre of Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: The first check-point was -- one of them was at the old bridge and the other one was at Nezuci.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This first one I think you mentioned, I think you said Medzedza, how far out of the town was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Around 11 kilometres, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you mentioned people making everyone get out of the bus. Can you describe those people or do you know the organisation that they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Well, this was the JNA troops, with some Serb locals. It was a mixture.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you've made reference to several check-points. Can you simply tell us how many check-points in total you encountered on your trip from Gorazde until the time you returned to your home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: I believe that, if my memory serves me well, that I mentioned five check-points, namely Medzedza, Nezuci, the old bridge, and the one outside new hotel in Visegrad and the one at Bikavac.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was your -- were you ever required to show your identification papers at any of these check-points?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes, at every check-point, they asked us to produce our identity cards and they had some sorts of lists against which they checked our papers and in respect of me, they said, in respect of me personally, "This is not him. He is not on this list."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And that happened at every check-point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Drawing your attention specifically to the check-point in front of the new hotel, who manned or who staffed that particular check-point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: At that check-point, outside the Novi hotel, the new hotel in Visegrad, there was standing a soldier by the name of Oliver Krsmanovic, who checked my papers very often. He was in a camouflage uniform and wore a kokarde with a two-headed eagle, and of armaments he had a heckler gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were there any JNA soldiers present at this particular check-point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes, they could be noticed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you returned to your home, could I ask you to describe what you found there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: When I returned to my home, I saw that the door had been broken, the house had been searched, not only my house but the entire settlement had been treated as it were in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The particular settlement that you lived in, was it predominantly one ethnicity or another or was it mixed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: It was mixed. There were Serbs and there were Muslims living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were the Serb homes that you saw, were they similarly damaged when you entered your neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So the damage was confined to the Muslim homes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, VG-014, did there come a time when you returned to your job?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If you are able to tell us the place where you worked without compromising your identity, I'd ask you to do so.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: I worked for a construction company, and my actual workplace was some 200 metres before one reached the new bridge, downstream the Drina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it was essentially in the centre of the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Well, not exactly in the very centre, but a bit farther away, the seat of the company was in the town proper; but my workplace where I worked was about 2 kilometres away from that spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you were going to and from work, did you have to go through check-points?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes, I had to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And were the procedures that you've already described, were the procedures similar on these repeated occasions that you went through the check-points? Did you hear the question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: I didn't have the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me repeat the question. You've mentioned that you've -- you went through check-points to get to work. Was the procedure that you've described for us already, was that same procedure followed when you went through the check-points to and from work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe what the conditions were like at work when you returned there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: The conditions were not good. We worked under stress. It wasn't safe to work, and you could even see soldiers passing by and things like that, so we were afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've said it was not safe to work. Could I ask you to explain what you mean precisely by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: It wasn't safe because people would enter the company premises and they took people away. They executed them. We didn't feel safe. And we had to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the people that were taken away from the workplace, were they of the same ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: They were Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was there any logic that you could decipher with respect to who was taken away and when?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Well, the logic was probably because we were Muslims. I don't see any other logic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I mean in terms of seniority or the place or the role that someone had in the community. Was there any logic to distinguish between the order in which Muslims were taken away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Look, first they took away people who did have some important positions and they probably did that so that they couldn't organise the people, and then when they finished that, then they moved to the people who were less educated.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you decided or reached the conclusion that it was no longer safe for you to go to work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How long was the period of time from when you returned to work and when you decided you could no longer go to work safely?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: I think that this was for a month or so. That was about the length of the period.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What did you do when you stopped going to work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: I was hiding close to the house in a small wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And were you hiding alone or with other people? Please don't tell us the names of the people but just, if you were, how many people.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes. There were three of my neighbours there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How did you eat or change your clothes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Our wives had organised things in such a way that at favourable times, they would bring us food and clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did your wife remain in your home with your child?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did your wife give you information about what was taking place in the town and in the Bikavac area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes. She said that the White Eagles were going through the settlement or the neighbourhood and were taking people away.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you did, in fact, simply return to your home, leave the woods and return to your home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes. I think that this was after about 10 days of hiding.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And why did you stop hiding in the woods?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: We couldn't take the conditions of the hiding any longer, and I thought that because I wasn't any criminal or I hadn't done anything bad, I didn't think that anyone would take me away.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you were forcibly taken from your home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How many nights had you spent in your home between the time you returned to your home and the time that you were forcibly taken from your home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Only one night.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And that one night, where did you stay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: In the attic of my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please describe for us what happened the day you were forcibly taken from your home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes. This was on the 7th of June 1992, in the evening, around 5.30 p.m. I was sitting at home and actually my wife saw through the kitchen that some soldiers were moving around through the neighbourhood and were searching the houses, and she suggested that I hide, but I refused to do that. Somebody knocked on the door. I said to a woman who had been expelled from the village of Kurtalici to go and see who it is and to say that there was no one at home, but when she went outside, probably because she was afraid, she couldn't speak, and I heard someone say that he would enter the house to check. And I was sitting there when Milan Lukic entered with a sniper in his hand, and he was -- his face was blackened and he had a Blue Beret on his head and he was wearing a blue uniform, and he had the kokarde and the double-headed eagle on the cap and he had the same insignia on his chest.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me ask a few questions here, just to ensure that the record is clear as to your testimony. How many people entered your home that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Only Milan Lukic came inside the house that day, and one of his soldiers was outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You're using the name of the person or calling this person by name. Did you know this person from before this day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: No. Lukic called him Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm not talking about Montenegro. I'm talking about the person you're referring to, Milan Lukic. Did you know him before this day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What was the name of the school that you attended?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: We went to secondary school together.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was he in the same year of school as you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: I think that he was in the same year, but we weren't in the same class.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you know what programme of study he was taking?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: I think it was the metal processing trade. I don't know if he was going to learn -- if he was learning to be a welder or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And for what length of time were you in the same school as this person you're referring to as Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: We were together for the first two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did there come a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Give us the years, if you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell us the years that you were in school with Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Well, just give me a moment. In 1985, I completed school, the third level, maybe 1983, 1984, I think that's the year that that would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when he left school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes. I think this was in the second year of high school sometime, or secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you know where he went?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: I heard that he went to Obrenovac, to be in the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, when you say you knew him in school, did you simply recognise that he was another boy in school with you or did you actually know his name at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes. I knew him from seeing him around, when he was a boy, but I also knew him by name.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you know where, what area, he came from, where his family lived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes. He was from the village of Rujiste.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've said that you were in different programmes of study. Can you tell us under what circumstances in school you would see Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: When the bell would ring for the break, all the students were outside in the yard or in the halls of the school, so -- in the corridors, so that's how we could see each other and spend time together.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe your impression of him as a boy in school with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes. He was a quiet boy. He didn't have any kind of attitude in terms of other ethnic groups. He was a nice boy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I want to take you back to the 7th of June, and you've made -- you testified that you saw him enter your house. My question for you is: How long did it take you to recognise the person that walked into your house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: It didn't take long. As soon as he came in, I recognised him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've testified that he had some black markings on his face. Did that give you concern that maybe it wasn't the person that you thought it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: No. I didn't have any doubts about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want you now to describe, as carefully as you can, what you remember about his appearance on that day. You've begun to describe some of the things he was wearing, but I would ask you if you could now just enumerate for us everything you remember about how he appeared to you that day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: When he entered my house, I already said that he was wearing a blue camouflage uniform. He had a police insignia on his arm. I don't remember which one but I do remember seeing it there. He had a black face, and then he had the kokarde and the double-headed eagle on his cap, and he had white sneakers on his feet, and on one of his arms he had a band-aid on the vein in the crook of the arm. He also had a mole on one side of his face, above the lip.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You mentioned white trainers. Do you recall if he was wearing socks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: He wasn't wearing socks, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've mentioned a band-aid on his arm. Could I ask you to indicate for us using your arm, your best memory of where you saw that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes. [Indicates]. It was here, like this, on the vein. It's usually the place where one would have their blood taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could the record reflect that the witness has pointed to the inside of his right forearm, just below the elbow.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, earlier you described the gun or weapon that he had. Could I ask you to describe it with a little greater specificity now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: It was a sniper with a silencer. Well, the calibre I'm not able to say right now. I'm a little bit forgetful, but I do know that it was a sniper with a silencer, in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was there anything unusual about his demeanour or the way he was acting that you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Please describe.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: When he entered my house, the first thing he did was to ask what we had in the house. Actually, he asked me my name, and I told him. He asked what did I have in the house? I told him to look, that I have the JNA reserve forces uniform. He went around, searched the house, and told me to take the uniform and to go with him. He acted as if he didn't know me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What were the lighting conditions in your home at the time that Mr. Milan Lukic came into your home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yeah. It was daylight. It was 5.30 p.m. in June. So you can imagine what the light was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was there anything obstructing your view of Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Where were you precisely in your home when he first walked into your home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: I was sitting on the couch behind the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And how far away was he from you when you first saw him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Well, if I were to stretch my arm out, I would have been able to touch him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You told us earlier that his face was blackened. Can you tell us with what was it blackened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know. It wasn't any kind of grease paint. It could have been some kind of soot or something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How much of his face had that black soot on it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only the face, around the eyes, cheeks. It wasn't thickly applied, this black-grey stuff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: On those parts of his face that had this black stuff on it, could you see the underlying skin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is it that made you recognise him, as you told the Prosecutor, immediately as he came in? What was there about his appearance that made you recognise him so quickly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The mask that was on his face wasn't something that would conceal his face so that you couldn't tell who it was. It was very easy to recognise him, and as I said earlier, he also had a mole on his face, and I knew him anyway from before; and I'm the kind of person who if I see a person once or twice, I always am able to recall that face later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You say that he pretended that he didn't know you. Did you say anything to him to indicate that you knew him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was afraid because if I let him know that I knew him, perhaps he would have killed me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Returning back to the -- your secondary school years, can you give us an approximation of either by how many times per week or how many times per month you would have seen Milan Lukic while you were at school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: We had five or six classes a day, and if we multiply that by five days, let's say that there were at least five classes a day, that was at least 25 classes a week, and then there is a break after each one or in between the classes, which are 45 minutes long each. So there is plenty of time to socialize and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So am I right in concluding that you -- your testimony is that you saw him during the breaks between the classes and you had approximately 25 classes per week?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And how many years were you in school at the same time that Milan Lukic was in school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: I said earlier that it was two years. I think at the end of the second year, I think, he left for Obrenovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I just want to return to something you testified a few moments ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, just a minute. I'm sorry, I'd like to find out from the witness whether he had a speaking relationship with Milan Lukic while he was at school. Was he somebody with whom you spoke normally, with whom you had conversations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He was not a friend of yours, then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, what about the period after school?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I can inquire about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You haven't come do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I hadn't intended but I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Go ahead, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How many students in your year of school can you approximate, how many students altogether were in your year?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Well, that takes a bit more calculation, but if I were to give a number, I would say 300 to 400 times in either school shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think there may have been some mistranslation. I'll ask my question again. I'm asking you how many students altogether were in your year at school? Not how many times you saw him over the course of the year but simply how many students altogether were in your year at school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This is what I meant when I said that in one school year, there were 300 to 400 students in both shifts, the first and the second shift, in school. Yes, that's how I understood the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. You've testified that he left school, and I believe you said he left Visegrad. Is that your evidence, that he left Visegrad when he left school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And do you know where he went?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: I believe that he was in Obrenovac then.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: From the time he left school until the 7th of June 1992, had you had any other occasions to see him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, did there come a time when you were taken from your apartment or your home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes, there did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Approximately how long were you with -- were you in your home -- or was Milan Lukic in your home before you were taken from it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: After this hiding, I spent the night at my place. This one night. And then Lukic came and he took me out of the house, if that is what you meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The time period I'm asking you for is from the time that Milan Lukic entered your home until the time you were taken from your home, how long is that period of time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: I believe that lasted for about ten minutes or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: When he ordered me to take my uniform, we set out towards the car, which was parked outside on the road and which was guarded by a soldier of his.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That soldier, did you recognise that soldier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What happened when you arrived at the car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Before we reached the car, itself, my wife and my daughter were standing in the doorway. I asked Milan Lukic to allow me to go back and to kiss my daughter and wife, and he refused to let me go. I disregarded his refusal and at my own initiative I went back and I kissed my wife and my daughter and then I went back towards the car. When I got near the car, Lukic opened the boot of the Passat car which he was driving. He put the uniform in the boot of the car, and he ordered us to sit in the rear, on the rear seat in the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Where was he when -- when the boot of the car was opened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: He was right behind the car, behind the boot of the car, where it is normal for one to stand when one opens the boot of the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Where were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: I was at the corner of the car, as it were, by his side.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you approximate the distance between you and him at this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Between half a metre and a metre.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you yourself put the uniform in the car or did he do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: I believe that I've said in my statement that it was he, it was him, who did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe the car for us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes. It was a Passat. It was the property of Behija Zukic, whom Lukic had killed before that and taken her car. It was of Burgundy colour, and that was that Passat vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you know -- did you know this car before -- or had you seen this car before this day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes. While it was the property of Behija Zukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you know Behija Zukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was this car similar to other cars in town, or that you had seen in town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Well, at that time, I believe that it was the only one of its kind, the one owned by Behija Zukic, that is, that was such a Passat make car.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You said "we" were placed in the car. When you say "we," who else are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Amir Kurtalic was also there, a friend of mine and of my family, who had also fled from the village of Kurtalici because it wasn't safe there. When we got out of my house, Lukic caught sight of Amir Kurtalic and then he told him, "You too come with me." And he told him to -- Kurtalic said, "Let my take my identity card." And Lukic told him, "You need no identity card. I am your identity card."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The Passat car, can I ask to you tell us how many people can sit in the Passat car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: In the back, three people can sit, one person can sit next to the driver, and with the driver it's five people all in all that can fit into it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How many people can sit in the front of the car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: The driver and the co-driver or the person sitting next to the driver, two people.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That would mean three people in the back of the car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Where were you sitting in the car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Amir Kurtalic and I were sitting in the back seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And were you sitting behind the driver's seat or behind the other seat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: I think that I was in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And where was Amir Kurtalic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: I think that he was on my right side, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did Milan Lukic get into the car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Where was he sitting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: He was actually driving the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did anyone else get into the car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes. His soldier who was standing -- who had been standing by the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was there a space between the two front seats on the car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes. There was a space around the gear shift lever where Lukic actually put his rifle, and he placed it so that the rifle barrel actually was pointing at my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you able to see -- were you able to see him while the car -- while you were driving in the car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes, I was able to see his back.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Where did the car go?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, before you move on to that point, I wanted to ask the witness -- Witness, you told us that this car was the property of Behija Zukic, that Lukic had killed her and he had taken her car. How did you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, I have said in my statement that this is something that I did not personally see for myself but this is something that I heard from my fellow citizens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When did you hear that first?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot recall with precision but I believe a day or two after the murder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When was that? In relation to your incident, can you tell us when that murder took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot specify the date, and the day; but I believe that it was some 10 days or so before my own incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Tell us what you heard. Tell us exactly what you heard.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I heard was this: That Lukic had entered Behija's house, killed her and took her car. He had probably also asked for or looked for money, but I'm not quite sure because I didn't actually inquire much about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you happen to hear other stories about Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I heard other stories. I also heard that he had liquidated the Smajic family in the centre of town, in the neighbourhood called Jondja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I heard lots of things. There were two cases of fire, of arson. This is not what I put in my statement, so these are not things that I'm exactly sure of but if you insist, it's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So that it is -- it would be correct to say that prior to your incident, you had heard many stories about Mr. Lukic's conduct, unlawful conduct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, also prior to my own case, and after my own case as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've mentioned of these -- when Judge Robinson has asked you about some of the other accounts that you've heard, you've mentioned two fires. Was that something that you heard before you -- your incident or after?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: These two fires occurred after my own incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell us with as much precision as you can how many different incidents you heard Milan Lukic was involved prior to the 7th of June?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Well, I mentioned already this murder of Behija Zukic. That is one. And that I also stated in my statement. I did not refer to the murder of the Smajic family in my statement but I also heard that story and that it had been committed by him, but if you can put me a more detailed question to a more specific question, I could perhaps give you an answer, but at this moment, I cannot recall any details myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was your prior knowledge of hearing these stories the reason why you recognised the person who walked into your house on the 7th of June? Is that why you believed it was Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Why did you believe it was Milan Lukic who walked into your house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Because I recognised him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned the car leaving your neighbourhood or your -- the front of your house. Where did it go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: It went not far from my house and it took a turn into a side street, an adjacent street, where there was on the road a grey-coloured Yugo, and that's where he pulled up and stopped the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The grey-coloured Yugo, did you recognise that car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes. It was my neighbour's car.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell us his name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: I think that his name was Osman Dzafic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe for us what you saw when the car, the Passat pulled up beside this grey Yugo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes. Immediately after the -- after stopping the Passat, a soldier whom I knew, but I cannot remember his name, who came out from an adjacent house and was leading another five people towards the car, and I saw that as I was sitting in the car. That was happening on the left side of the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you know the name of the five people that were being led towards the car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Meho and Ekrem Dzafic, father and son. And then Hasan Mutapcic and Hasan Kustura and VG-032 were all there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were all of those men Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you -- how many of -- how many men were there that were not part of the group that was detained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Are you referring to the soldiers? If you are referring to the soldiers, there were three of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes. I was referring to the soldiers. Were they all armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In addition to the men that you saw there on the street, did you learn that there were other men being detained, other Muslim men being detained at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes. Later, I learned that there had remained another six men in that same house.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How long did you remain at that location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Well, we stayed at that particular location only until we got into the car, and then we continued on our journey.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you leave that location still in the Passat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes. I was still in the Passat in the same seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And was Amir Kurtalic still in the same seat in the Passat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Who drove the Passat at this stage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Milan Lukic did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Who was in the front passenger seat of the Passat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: The soldier of his.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was there anyone else in the Passat aside from you, Amir Kurtalic and the two people in the front?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes, from among the five men who had been taken to the spot, Hasan Mutapcic also sat in the Passat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was anyone placed in the grey Yugo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes. The remaining four men, together with a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Where did the car go this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: This time, we set out in the direction of the Vilina Vlas Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you estimate for us how long in kilometres the distance is from where the car left to the Vilina Vlas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Well, looking from the centre of the city, the distance to Vilina Vlas was five kilometres, plus this portion up there, so it's 5.5 kilometres all in all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you estimate for us how long it took you to drive from where you're mentioning now to the Vilina Vlas Hotel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say with precision but perhaps 20 or 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During that 20 or 25 minutes, were you in a position to see Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes, from the back, actually I could see his back.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did it ever occur to you while you were driving that perhaps it was not Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: On the way to the Vilina Vlas Hotel, did Milan Lukic ever stop the car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes. He did stop the car at a couple of places, when he had occasion to see a pedestrian, a man, he would stop the car and ask the man for his name, and when the man replied, he would tell him, "Oh, you are not a balija."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you use the word "balija", is that a derogatory term used to describe Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What happened when you arrived at Vilina Vlas Hotel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: When we arrived in front of the Vilina Vlas Hotel, Lukic ordered us out of the car and to get into the hotel. He ordered us to line up in front of the reception desk until he found the keys to the manager's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Prior to going into the hotel, was there a check-point that you passed through?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes, there was a check-point at the Sase crossroads.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what if anything happened at that check-point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes, something did happen. Passing by that check-point, Lukic, Milan Lukic, stopped the car and he said probably or, in fact, he did say to the Serbs, his Serbs there, that he had hunted himself a number of balijas.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Returning now to the Vilina Vlas Hotel, did you see anyone else that you recognised in the hotel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: At the hotel, I recognised Mitar Vasiljevic. He had an olive-drab uniform, black, large black hat with a kokarde and a double-headed eagle and he also had a red ribbon on his shoulder. He was armed. I also recognised Momir Savic. He was in a camouflage uniform, wore a large black hat with the same insignia, the two-headed eagle, and he also had a red ribbon on his shoulder. Also, I recognised this Susnjar, I don't know what his name, first name, was or is but I did recognise him because before the war he used to work as a security guard in the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How many men -- you're referring to as soldiers. How many men altogether are in the Vilina Vlas Hotel at this stage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Well, if you are referring to soldiers, there were three whom I recognised at the hotel, and then there were the three who had taken us to the hotel, so there were a total of six men.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And out of those six, you've testified that you recognised four of them from knowing them prior to this day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And as far as you know, the other two, you had never seen before the 7th of June?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You said you knew Mitar Vasiljevic. How did you know Mitar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes, I knew Mitar Vasiljevic well. He worked as a catering worker at the Panos hotel, and I would be there often because they had Bingo there and one would go there for a drink or to have a snack, so that I had occasion to have -- I had quite a few drinks with this self-same Mitar Vasiljevic so I knew him quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you actually interacted with Mitar Vasiljevic on a social -- in social terms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. When I stayed at the Panos, that's the way it was. We would have a drink or two together.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Of the six people you're referring to as soldiers in the Vilina Vlas Hotel, how many of them had black paint or black markings on their face similar to Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Well, I mentioned or in fact I did not mention this. The fact is that the soldier who came with Lukic to take me away, whom he called Montenegro, he had two streaks, to black streaks, on his cheeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How about the other men? Did they have any black markings on their face?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you said that Milan Lukic was looking for some keys. Can you please remind us what type of keys he was looking for and was he successful in finding them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, I believe that he was -- he asked Mitar Vasiljevic to give him the keys to the manager's office. He gave him some keys. He tried to open that office. He could not. And he was angry, and he just threw the keys into the corridor and he ordered us to get back into the cars and sit in the same way as we were sitting before.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were all of the men brought into the hotel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what part of the hotel were you all brought into?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: We were in the area in front of the reception.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you've testified that Milan Lukic ordered you and the other men that were detained to get back into the cars. Did you get back into the cars?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And approximately how long in total were you in the reception area of the hotel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. It seemed like an eternity, but we didn't really stay that long, maybe 15 or 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what was the lighting conditions in the reception area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: It was good, natural light, that entrance area was full of windows so there was no doubt about being able to see everyone clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And during the 15 or 20 minutes you estimate you were in the reception area, was Milan Lukic in the reception area that entire time as well, or did he leave for some period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: He was there in the corridor looking for the keys, and trying to open the manager's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: At any time were you or any of the other men blindfolded or made to turn around and face the wall?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, you're leading on important matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was there anything obstructing your view while you were in the reception area of the hotel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Which way were you facing while you were in the reception area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: We were all focused on Lukic and the soldiers, whether he would find the keys, whether we would be locked into that room or not. We were always looking at him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you did re-enter the cars?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Which car did you get into?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: I got into the same vehicle that I was brought to Vilina Vlas in, the Passat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did all of the people get into the same cars that they were in when they came to the Vilina Vlas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes. Only when we were leaving Vilina Vlas, we were joined by Mitar Vasiljevic too.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And which car did he get into?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: This time, Mitar Vasiljevic sat together with Lukic in the Passat and the soldier who had driven the vehicle to Vilina Vlas moved into the Yugo vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Who drove the vehicle to -- who drove the Passat to the Vilina Vlas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay, the transcript records your last answer as saying the soldier who had driven the vehicle to Vilina Vlas moved into the Yugo vehicle. Is that a correct recording of what you said about that man who moved to the Yugo vehicle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: No. I said that Milan drove from Bikavac to Vilina Vlas, and the soldier who was with him was sitting in the co-driver's seat, in the passenger seat, next to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And that's the person who moved into the grey Yugo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Where did the car go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: When we came back to the cars, they again drove us in the direction of Visegrad. We were returning by the same road, in the direction of Sase.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did there come a time when the cars stopped?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes. They did stop, after we passed the intersection at Sase and were driving along the road towards Prelovo, some 500 metres after they stopped the cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Am I correct in saying that the road from Vilina -- that there is a road that goes from Visegrad to Prelovo that travels roughly along the right bank of the Drina River?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that there is a road that travels from Vilina Vlas that intersects that road at a T junction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And in this trip from Vilina Vlas that you're now describing for us, did the car arrive at that T junction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes. Going along the road from Vilina Vlas towards the Sase intersection, in the conversation between Milan Lukic and Mitar Vasiljevic, actually Mitar Vasiljevic asked Lukic what are we going to do with them? And he replied, Lukic replied to Vasiljevic, that they were going to exchange us for 300 soldiers who had fallen at Zepa and driving along like that we reached the Sase intersection and continued along the road in the direction of Prelovo. At one point, Milan Lukic asked Mitar Vasiljevic, since he spotted a house on the right-hand side above the road, if it was a Muslim house, and this other man confirmed that it was, and that's where they stopped the cars, and he left the car, his soldiers also came out of the car, and ordered us also to come out of the vehicles. At that point in time, Milan Lukic said, I quote, "I don't want to hear a sound." And that we should start walking towards the Drina River. As we walked in the direction of the River Drina, in a column, one behind the other, we passed through a field which was planted with potatoes at the time, and we walked for a while, and then suddenly Milan Lukic ordered us to stop, some ten metres before we actually reached the river, which is what we did. And at that point in time, my village, my native village, was just across the river, so all my memories from early youth passed through my head at that time, and most of all -- I'm sorry. I held the image -- I'm sorry, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could the usher bring some tissues or something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could see an image of my underage daughter and my wife, who had stayed at home and saw me off with tears. Suddenly, my thoughts were interrupted by Milan Lukic's sharp voice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I had said we would break at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's perhaps a convenient time now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If the Court feels it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll break for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sounds like Mr. Cepic has an open mike. I can hear your conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: VG-014, before we recommence my questioning, I want to say the break we just took was, it had nothing to do with you getting upset. We recognise that this brings back traumatic memories and we certainly understand and hope that you don't feel embarrassed in any way. Just before the break, you were telling us that Milan Lukic, Mitar Vasiljevic, the other men, were bringing you and the other detained Muslim men down to the river bank. Can I ask you to continue now from the point in time when you're approaching the river bank?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes. At the time when we were -- at the point in time when we approached the river bank, some ten metres in front, Milan Lukic ordered us to stop. He asked which one of us was able to swim? We were all silent except for VG-032. He replied that he could swim. He ordered us in a sharp voice, raised voice, to start moving towards the river Drina bank and that no one should even attempt to escape because they would be killed. We did so. As we were getting close to the river bank, one behind the other in a line, I could see, and I also was able to sense that the end was coming. I still had an image of my daughter and my wife in my head, but what could I do? Nothing could be changed. At that moment, Meho Dzafic, Mitar Vasiljevic's colleague, was heard. He was begging Mitar Vasiljevic not to kill him because they were colleagues from work. Mitar Vasiljevic pretended not to know him. Then one of the soldiers asked how they should fire. Lukic said that they should fire individual shots. I could hear them cocking their weapons. For a moment everything went quiet. And then after a brief period of time, a shot ensued. After that first shot, I don't know if it was by instinct or how, I just fell down. I wasn't actually hit. I fell in a way that I actually turned by 180 degrees. We were standing facing the water and Lukic and his soldiers were behind our back, some five or six metres behind. When I fell in the water, I could hear the scream of one of my colleagues. I didn't know who it was. Then another shot was heard. Everything went quiet, and the person from the bank fell on top of me and on top of VG-032. I heard bodies jerking, and then everything went quiet for a moment. After a certain period of time, somebody came up to the bank and said, "Well, there is one of them that's alive. Why don't you go there?" I don't remember who said that, but there were two more shots close to my head, and there was a third shot which was a little bit farther away. And this was what happened there. Even after those two shots, I was still not hit, and I was listening, I didn't want to be surprised by shots or anything, so I was listening to see if they would go away. When I heard the doors of the vehicles closing, I slowly raised my head, I looked towards the bank, I could see there was nobody there, again I returned to the same position, and I had doubts that they had all left. I thought that somebody may have been left behind to see what would happen. But actually nobody was there, again I raised my head and on my left-hand side, VG-032 also stood up. I asked him if he was wounded and he said that he wasn't. He asked me if I was wounded, and I also told him that I wasn't either. And then I suggested that we should run from the place because before Lukic said that he had six more people to bring, and we were afraid that he would bring them to the same place, and so I and VG-032 stood up from the water. Before us there was the body of Hasan Mutapcic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I could ask you some specific questions about your ordeal, you said that you were lined up along the river. Were all the men -- which way were you facing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: We were lined up along the bank, and we were facing the water, the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you remember who was to your left or where you were in this line of people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes. Hasan Kustura was on my left-hand side and on my right-hand side, Hasan Mutapcic stood.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And do you know the position of the other men, the other four men? Are you able to say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes. I will go in the order that we reached the bank. Meho Dzafic was at the head of the column followed by his son Ekrem and then VG-032, followed by Hasan Mutapcic, VG-014, Hasan Kustura and Amir Kurtalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you were describing what happened, you talked about a conversation that seemed to concern the way the guns would be used. Could you please tell us exactly what you recall hearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: One of the soldiers asked, "How should we fire?" And Lukic said, "Individual shots." Could you could hear the weapons being cocked and the preparations for firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Am I correct in saying that you had some military -- you have done some military service, mandatory military service, as part of the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And are you familiar with weapons generally that can be found in the area of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've already described the gun that Milan Lukic had. Can you describe, if you recall, or identify, if you recall, the weapons that the other men had at the river?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes. I will start from Mitar Vasiljevic. He had a semi-automatic rifle, and the other two soldiers had automatic weapons. Milan Lukic, of course, had a sniper.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And when you say semi-automatic weapons, were they -- I mean sorry, automatic weapons, were they pistols or rifles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: No. We are talking about rifles, semi-automatic rifle and automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So when you heard the conversation, "How should we fire," and Milan Lukic saying, "Individual shots," what did you interpret that to mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Well, when he said, "Individual fire," I had a feeling then that he, Milan Lukic, and the rest of his soldiers were taking pleasure in killing because they had decided on individual fire, giving them time to aim at the person and kill them with relish, as we would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would someone have to do something to an automatic weapon to make it fire single shot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes. Automatic weapons have a kind of knob which you would have to put into position for individual fire or to return it to bursts of fire, so you could set it for individual or bursts of fire. In semi-automatic weapons, you don't need to do that. Semi-automatic weapons didn't have that knob or -- all you needed to do was to cock the weapon and there are ten bullets in a semi-automatic rifle, so you would fire the shots as long as you had the bullets to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: With respect to the automatic weapon, does it generate a sound when it is -- this knob that you described is moved from automatic mode to single-shot mode?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you could hear the click.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you hear the clicks that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When the gun -- when an automatic placed is semi- -- or in single shot mode, does that cause it to operate very similar to a semi-automatic weapon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-014
utterances.text: When you have an automatic weapon on single-shot mode, it can fire one bullet, depending on the speed of firing, depending on the speed of the person actually firing. That is the speed at which they can fire single shots.
